newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine 91-day T-bill rate rises to 9.583 pct.
newsitem.headline: Philippine 91-day T-bill rate rises to 9.583 pct.

text.p: The Philippine benchmark 91-day Treasury bill rate rose to an average of 9.583 percent at the regular weekly auction from 9.498 percent last week, the Bureau of Treasury said on Monday.

This is the first time the bellwether rate has corrected upwards after seven weeks of decline. This is also the fourth consecutive week the 91-day bill has been at single-digit levels since September 1995.
All the other maturities also adjusted upwards. The 181-day T-bill rate edged up to an average of 10.057 from 9.842 percent; and the 363-day rate climbed to 10.555 from 10.388 percent.
The auction had 13.540 billion pesos worth of tenders, of which 4.5 billion pesos were awarded.
The rally in the T-bill rates was expected after the Central Bank started selling on Thursday six-month reverse repos at a higher-than-market rate of 10.125 percent, dealers said.
"That was the clincher," a foreign bank trader said, because the Central Bank sent a signal to the market that it did not want rates to go down further.
Bankers said domestic interest rates had fallen too low and it did not attract arbitrage money anymore and prodded the Central Bank to move accordingly.
After the Central Bank's move, overseas funds had started coming back, a dealer said.

Central Bank Treasurer Sergio Edeza told Reuters after the auction "It's too early to tell," when asked whether he thought interest rates had bottomed out. "We have to wait for the next few auctions."
"Yes, we're comfortable with both the exchange rate and the interest rate," Edeza said, referring to the current levels.
A Bureau of Treasury official acknowledged that the uptick in domestic interest rates was due to the Central Bank's action.
The official said the higher-than-market six-month reverse repos were intended to siphon more liquidity from banks since money supply levels were edging closer to the programmed ceilings.
Last Friday, the Central Bank reported that base and reserve money were 10 billion pesos below their targets in March.

These money supply levels were, however, 20 billion pesos below their ceilings in February. The ceilings were set as part of an International Monetary Fund programme from which the country expects to exit in June this year.
